lessons.title: How to interview
lessons.explain: Interviewers score your PROCESS, not just the answer. Clarify the problem, state your approach out loud, start with brute force, then optimize, and communicate trade-offs.
lessons.example: Clarify → approach out loud → brute force → optimize → test → discuss
objectives: Communicate your reasoning clearly while solving a problem live
Explain how think aloud changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect think aloud with clarify and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
commonMistakes: Staying silent while thinking during a live interview, leaving the interviewer no way to follow your reasoning or help.

lessons.title: Behavioral interviews & the STAR method
objectives: Structure a behavioral answer using the STAR method
Explain how STAR method changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect STAR method with situation/task/action/result and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Behavioral interviews probe past experience to predict future behavior ('tell me about a time you disagreed with a teammate'). The STAR method structures a clear answer: Situation (brief context), Task (what needed to happen), Action (what YOU specifically did), Result (the outcome, ideally with a concrete measure).
examples:
# STAR in practice:
# Situation: 'Our team's deploy pipeline was failing intermittently'
# Task: 'I needed to find the root cause before the next release'
# Action: 'I added logging, isolated it to a race condition, and fixed it'
# Result: 'Deploy failures dropped from 15% to under 1%'
commonMistakes: Describing what 'the team' did throughout a STAR answer instead of specifically what YOU did — interviewers are evaluating your individual judgment and actions, not the team's.
lessons.careerRelevance: STAR-structured answers are the expected format in virtually every behavioral interview round across company types.
lessons.explain: Behavioral interviews probe past experience to predict future behavior ('tell me about a time you disagreed with a teammate'). # STAR in practice:

# Task: 'I needed to find the root cause before the next release'

lessons.title: Technical interviews: what's actually being evaluated
objectives: Understand what a technical interviewer is really scoring beyond 'right answer'
Explain how process over pure output changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect process over pure output with communicated reasoning and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A technical interview scores more than just reaching a correct final answer: how you clarify the problem before coding, whether you communicate your reasoning as you go, how you handle hints or pushback, and whether you test/verify your own solution.
examples:
# what's actually being scored:
# - clarifying questions before diving in
# - reasoning communicated OUT LOUD, not just silent typing
# - responding well to hints, not getting defensive
# - testing your own solution before declaring it done
commonMistakes: Treating a technical interview as a silent exam to be solved alone — interviewers are actively evaluating your communication and collaboration throughout, not just grading a final answer.
lessons.careerRelevance: This process-focused framing directly connects to the Problem Solving track's think-aloud practice.

lessons.title: Whiteboard & live problem-solving interviews
objectives: Apply a structured approach to solving a problem live, under observation
Explain how narrated problem-solving changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect narrated problem-solving with managing observation pressure and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Live problem-solving (whiteboard or shared editor) rewards the same method as the Problem Solving track: restate the problem, work a small example, identify the pattern, start with brute force, then optimize — done OUT LOUD, in front of the interviewer, rather than silently in your head.
examples:
# live problem-solving flow, narrated out loud:
# 'Let me make sure I understand -- so we want the longest subarray where...'
# 'Let me try a small example: [1,2,3] would give...'
# 'I'll start with a brute-force approach, then see if we can optimize'
commonMistakes: Going silent for long stretches while thinking — even when stuck, narrating your current thinking ('I'm considering whether a hash map helps here') keeps the interviewer engaged and gives.
lessons.careerRelevance: Comfort with being watched while thinking is a distinct, practicable skill separate from raw problem-solving ability.
lessons.explain: Live problem-solving (whiteboard or shared editor) rewards the same method as the Problem Solving track: restate the problem, work a small example, identify the pattern, start with brute force, then optimize — done OUT LOUD, in front of the interviewer, rather than silently in your head.

lessons.title: System design interviews
objectives: Structure a system design interview answer
Explain how requirements clarification first changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect requirements clarification first with high-level then deep-dive and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: System design interviews (common for more senior roles, sometimes appearing even at internship level) evaluate architectural judgment on open-ended problems ('design a URL shortener').
examples:
# system design flow:
# 1. clarify: how many users? read-heavy or write-heavy? latency requirements?
# 2. sketch high-level: client -> load balancer -> API -> database (+ cache)
# 3. go deep where the interviewer leans in, discussing trade-offs explicitly
commonMistakes: Jumping straight into deep technical detail on one component before clarifying scale and requirements — the 'right' design depends entirely on requirements that must be established first.
lessons.careerRelevance: System design interview structure directly reuses the System Design track's content, applied under live interview conditions.

lessons.title: Mock interview workflow
objectives: Design and run an effective mock interview practice routine
Explain how realistic simulation changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect realistic simulation with specific actionable feedback and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: An effective mock interview practice loop: simulate real conditions (timed, out loud, ideally with another person rather than silently in your head), get specific feedback (not just 'good job' but what exactly worked or didn't), and iterate — targeting the SPECIFIC weakness identified, not just repeating generic practice.
examples:
# mock interview loop:
# 1. simulate real conditions: timed, verbal, with a partner or recording
# 2. get SPECIFIC feedback ('you jumped to coding before clarifying constraints')
# 3. practice that SPECIFIC weakness deliberately before the next mock
# 4. repeat, tracking improvement over successive mocks
commonMistakes: Doing many mock interviews with no specific feedback loop or targeted improvement focus — repetition without a feedback loop plateaus quickly; targeted iteration on named weaknesses.
lessons.careerRelevance: A deliberate mock-interview practice discipline is one of the highest-leverage, most controllable parts of interview preparation.

lessons.title: Communication skills in interviews
objectives: Apply concrete communication habits that improve interview performance
Explain how deliberate pacing changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect deliberate pacing with clarifying over guessing and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Strong interview communication is learnable and concrete: pause briefly before answering rather than rushing to fill silence, ask clarifying questions rather than guessing at ambiguous prompts, and check in periodically ('does this approach make sense so far?') rather than talking uninterrupted for minutes.
examples:
# concrete communication habits:
# - a 2-3 second pause before answering beats a rushed, unclear answer
# - 'to make sure I understand correctly...' before diving into an ambiguous prompt
# - periodic check-ins during a long explanation, not one uninterrupted monologue
commonMistakes: Treating communication skill as fixed/innate rather than a practicable habit — these are concrete, learnable behaviors, not just personality traits.
lessons.careerRelevance: Communication quality is explicitly and separately scored in most structured interview rubrics, alongside technical correctness.
lessons.explain: Strong interview communication is learnable and concrete: pause briefly before answering rather than rushing to fill silence, ask clarifying questions rather than guessing at ambiguous prompts, and check in periodically ('does this approach make sense so far?') rather than talking uninterrupted for minutes.

lessons.title: Salary negotiation basics
objectives: Apply basic, low-risk negotiation practices after receiving an offer
Explain how market research before negotiating changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect market research before negotiating with total package framing and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Negotiation basics: let the company name a number first when possible, research a realistic market range beforehand (from public salary-data sources and your own network) so you have a concrete anchor, and negotiate the TOTAL package (base, equity, signing bonus, start date) not just base salary alone.
examples:
# a low-risk, low-drama negotiation script:
# 'Thank you for the offer, I'm excited about this. Based on my research and other
# conversations, I was hoping for something closer to $X -- is there flexibility here?'
commonMistakes: Accepting the very first offer immediately with no attempt to ask about flexibility — a polite, well-researched ask rarely costs anything and often yields at least a modest improvement.
lessons.careerRelevance: Negotiation directly affects real compensation outcomes and is a skill worth practicing deliberately, not avoiding out of discomfort.
lessons.explain: Negotiation basics: let the company name a number first when possible, research a realistic market range beforehand (from public salary-data sources and your own network) so you have a concrete anchor, and negotiate the TOTAL package (base, equity, signing bonus, start date) not just base salary alone.
lessons.example:
# a low-risk, low-drama negotiation script:
# 'Thank you for the offer, I'm excited about this. Based on my research and other
# conversations, I was hoping for something closer to $X -- is there flexibility here?'

lessons.title: Follow-up emails & closing the loop
objectives: Write an effective post-interview follow-up email
Explain how timely follow-up changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect timely follow-up with specific over generic and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A brief, genuine follow-up email within a day of each interview round — thanking the specific interviewer, referencing one real detail from the conversation, and reaffirming interest — is a small, low-cost signal of genuine engagement that a surprising number of candidates skip entirely.
examples:
# generic (weak): 'Thank you for your time today. I look forward to hearing from you.'
# specific (stronger): 'Thanks for walking me through the caching challenges your team is
# tackling -- our conversation about the trade-offs there really stuck with me.'
commonMistakes: Sending no follow-up at all, or a generic template identical to what you'd send any company — a brief, specific note costs little time and measurably signals genuine engagement.
lessons.careerRelevance: This is a small, easy, frequently-skipped habit with outsized signal value relative to its low effort cost.
lessons.explain: A brief, genuine follow-up email within a day of each interview round — thanking the specific interviewer, referencing one real detail from the conversation, and reaffirming interest — is a small, low-cost signal of genuine engagement that a surprising number of candidates skip entirely.
lessons.example:
# generic (weak): 'Thank you for your time today. I look forward to hearing from you.'
# specific (stronger): 'Thanks for walking me through the caching challenges your team is
# tackling -- our conversation about the trade-offs there really stuck with me.'

quiz.q: Interviewers mainly evaluate:
options: only the final answer
your reasoning process
typing speed
memorization

quiz.q: STAR is a framework for:
options: coding
behavioral answers
SQL
system design

quiz.q: The STAR method's 'A' stands for:
options: Answer
Action -- specifically what YOU did
Assessment
Ask

quiz.q: A technical interviewer typically also evaluates:
options: only the final correct answer
communicated reasoning and process, not just the final answer
typing speed
handwriting on the whiteboard

quiz.q: A good system design interview answer starts with:
options: diving into database schema details
clarifying requirements and scale
writing code immediately
picking a cloud provider

quiz.q: What does STAR stand for?
options: Skills, Tasks, Actions, Results
Situation, Task, Action, Result
Strategy, Timing, Analysis, Review
Structure, Test, Apply, Reflect

quiz.q: What is the purpose of the 'Situation' part of STAR?
options: stating the final outcome
establishing context so the interviewer understands the circumstances
listing your skills
asking a clarifying question

quiz.q: What is the purpose of the 'Result' part of STAR?
options: describing the context only
concretely stating the outcome and impact of your actions
asking a follow-up question
describing what you would do differently with no real outcome given

quiz.q: In a technical interview, what's often being evaluated beyond just the final correct answer?
options: nothing else matters besides the final answer
your process, communicated reasoning, and how you respond to hints along the way
only how fast you type
only whether you've memorized the exact problem before

quiz.q: Why think out loud during a technical/whiteboard interview?
options: thinking aloud is generally discouraged
it lets the interviewer follow your reasoning and offer guidance, rather than sitting in silence guessing what you're doing
interviewers only care about the final code, never the process
silence is always preferred during live coding

quiz.q: Why write a brute-force solution first in a live coding interview?
options: brute force is always the expected final answer
it demonstrates a working baseline and correct understanding before attempting to optimize, reducing risk of an incomplete broken 'clever' solution
brute force should never be mentioned out loud
optimizing first is always safer

quiz.q: Why manage observation pressure by narrating your process?
options: narrating increases pressure further
articulating your thinking transforms silent anxiety into a structured, visible problem-solving process the interviewer can engage with
staying silent always reduces pressure more effectively
observation pressure has no real effect on interview performance

quiz.q: In a system design interview, what should typically happen before diving into details?
options: immediately drawing a detailed architecture diagram
clarifying requirements and constraints first
picking a specific database technology immediately
refusing to ask any questions

quiz.q: Why discuss trade-offs explicitly in a system design interview?
options: trade-offs should be avoided entirely
real system design always involves trade-offs, and articulating them shows genuine understanding rather than reciting a memorized 'correct' design
there is always one single objectively correct design
trade-off discussion only matters for junior candidates

quiz.q: What makes mock interview feedback most useful?
options: vague overall impressions
specific, actionable feedback tied to particular moments, which can be targeted in further practice
feedback focused only on whether you passed or failed
feedback given without any specific examples

quiz.q: Why iterate with targeted practice after a mock interview, rather than just repeating full mocks?
options: repeating identical mocks is always more effective
targeting specific weak areas identified in feedback makes practice time more efficient than repeating the same full simulation
targeted practice has no real benefit over generic repetition
mock interviews shouldn't be followed by any specific follow-up practice

quiz.q: Why use deliberate pacing when answering interview questions?
options: speaking as fast as possible is always better
rushing can lead to incomplete or garbled answers, while deliberate pacing helps you communicate clearly and think as you speak
pacing has no effect on how answers are perceived
interviewers prefer answers given with no pauses at all

quiz.q: Why clarify rather than guess when a question is ambiguous?
options: guessing is always the safer choice
clarifying ensures you're solving the actual intended problem, rather than wasting effort on a misunderstood version of it
clarifying questions are seen as a sign of weakness
ambiguous questions should be skipped entirely

quiz.q: Why do periodic check-ins during a long answer or problem help?
options: check-ins are unnecessary interruptions
they confirm you're still aligned with what the interviewer is looking for, catching misunderstandings early rather than at the end
check-ins always signal a lack of confidence
interviewers prefer no interaction until the very end

quiz.q: Why research market rates before a salary negotiation?
options: market research is unnecessary, any number works
knowing realistic market rates lets you negotiate from an informed, credible position rather than guessing
market research only matters for senior roles
salary is never actually negotiable regardless of research

quiz.q: Why frame a negotiation around total package rather than base salary alone?
options: base salary is the only thing that matters
total compensation (bonus, equity, benefits) often has significant value beyond the base number alone
total package framing is a manipulation tactic to avoid using
benefits and equity are never negotiable

quiz.q: What does 'low-risk asking' mean in salary negotiation?
options: asking is inherently always risky and harmful
politely and professionally asking for more rarely damages an offer, since most companies expect some negotiation
asking for more always results in an offer being withdrawn
negotiation should never be attempted under any circumstances

quiz.q: Why send a timely follow-up email after an interview?
options: timing has no effect on how a follow-up is received
promptness signals genuine continued interest and keeps you fresh in the interviewer's mind
follow-ups should always be delayed as long as possible
follow-up emails are never read by interviewers

quiz.q: Why reference something specific from the interview in a follow-up, rather than a generic thank-you?
options: specificity has no real advantage over a generic message
referencing a specific detail demonstrates genuine engagement and memorable authenticity, rather than a copy-paste template
generic messages are always more professional
specific references risk seeming presumptuous

quiz.q: Why is a follow-up email considered a 'low-cost genuine signal'?
options: it costs significant time and resources to send
it takes little effort to send but can meaningfully reinforce your interest and professionalism at minimal cost
follow-up emails require extensive preparation
the signal value of a follow-up is negligible

quiz.q: What does 'responsiveness to hints' evaluate in a technical interview?
options: whether you ignore all interviewer input
how well you incorporate interviewer guidance and adjust your approach, rather than rigidly sticking to a failing path
hints are never given in real technical interviews
responsiveness is irrelevant to the evaluation

quiz.q: Why might 'process over pure output' matter more in some technical interviews than the final answer alone?
options: process is never actually evaluated
how you approach and reason through a problem often predicts real on-the-job performance better than one isolated final answer
only the final answer is ever relevant
process only matters for junior-level candidates

quiz.q: Why simulate realistic conditions during mock interview practice?
options: realism has no bearing on how useful practice is
practicing under conditions similar to the real interview (time pressure, live coding, verbal explanation) better prepares you for the actual experience
mock interviews should always be easier than the real thing
realistic simulation only matters for behavioral interviews

quiz.q: Why avoid vague, generic answers when using the STAR method?
options: vague answers are always sufficient
specific, concrete details (real situations, real outcomes) are far more convincing and memorable than generic, generalized descriptions
STAR doesn't require any specific details
generic answers demonstrate stronger communication skills

quiz.q: Why is 'clarify' listed as an early step in effective interviewing behavior?
options: clarifying is a sign of unpreparedness
confirming your understanding of the actual question before diving in prevents wasted effort solving the wrong problem
clarifying should only happen after finishing your answer
interviewers always state questions unambiguously so clarifying is never needed
